If q is placed to the left of (2,0), for example between the origin and (2,0), then the electric field produced by q at (2,0) also points in the +x direction, in the same direction as the electric field of Q, so the magnitude of the resultant electric field increases. If q is placed to the right of (2,0), then the electric field produced by q at (2,0) points in the -x direction, opposite to the electric field of Q; if q is placed far enough away, this reverse electric field is smaller than the original electric field of Q, so the magnitude of the resultant electric field will decrease compared with before. Therefore, |E| can increase or decrease depending on the position of q.

Since the electric field from a positive charge points away from that charge, the field from Q at (2,0) points in the +x direction. If q is placed to the left of (2,0), for example between the origin and (2,0), its field at (2,0) also points +x, so the magnitude increases. If q is placed to the right of (2,0), its field at (2,0) points -x; choosing it far enough away makes this opposing field smaller than the original field from Q, so the resultant magnitude decreases. method.method_draft: Use a vector-magnitude comparison. From the image, identify the observation point (2,0) and Q at the origin, so the original field is E_Q = kQ/2^2 in the +x direction. From the text, q is a positive charge whose location can vary. Let q be at a general point (a,b). Its field at (2,0) is proportional to the vector from q to the observation point, (2-a, -b), divided by the cube of the distance. Compare the new magnitude using |E_Q + E_q|^2 = |E_Q|^2 + 2 E_Q · E_q + |E_q|^2. If q is placed so that E_q has a positive x-component, the dot product term is positive and the field magnitude increases. If q is placed to the right of (2,0), E_q has a negative x-component; for a sufficiently weak opposing field, the negative dot product term can outweigh |E_q|^2, causing the magnitude to decrease. Thus the sign of the change depends on q's position.
